title: How Will AI Shake Up Your Growth Strategy?
gist: BCG's study of 3,669 large public companies finds AI-linked growth initiatives more than doubled (4.9% to 12.7%) after GenAI, and proposes a 2x2 of AI disruption risk vs. AI opportunity yielding four growth strategies: catch the wave, reinvent the core, pivot beyond the core, and step up your game. Capability/knowledge-based moats (e.g., CRM/ERP software, BPO) are most exposed, while position-based moats (brands, scarce assets) are more protected.

insights.claim: BCG's analysis of 3,669 public companies with over $1B revenue found the share mentioning AI in connection with growth initiatives more than doubled from 4.9% (2017–2022) to 12.7% (2023–2025) after generative AI went mainstream.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: AI-for-growth disclosure is still a minority behavior (~1 in 8 large growers), so early adopters may still be building differentiated advantage.
insights.quote: the share of companies mentioning AI in connection with growth initiatives more than doubled from 4.9% before GenAI to 12.7% after
insights.locator: We then analyzed their corporate announcements

insights.claim: Companies that sustained, accelerated, or reignited above-average growth leveraged AI significantly more in the GenAI era than those delivering below-average growth, making AI adoption a marker of growth leadership.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: Screen for AI-linked growth initiatives in shareholder communications as a possible leading indicator of sustained outperformance.
insights.locator: We then analyzed their corporate announcements

insights.claim: Among growth outperformers, 90% of semiconductor companies and 75% of software companies discussed AI in relation to growth, while capital goods rose from 2% to 15% and utilities from 1% to 11% between the pre- and post-GenAI periods.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: AI-linked growth is spreading from tech into industrials and utilities — the AI build-out narrative is broadening into old-economy sectors.
insights.quote: 15% of capital goods companies reported AI use in the AI era, up from 2% in the earlier period—as did 11% of utilities, up from 1%
insights.locator: Even among outperformers, the level of AI adoption

insights.claim: Strong growers in sectors with low AI opportunity and low disruption risk are ten times more likely to embrace AI for growth than their underperforming peers in the same sectors.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: Even in 'AI-neutral' sectors, AI adoption separates winners from laggards — useful for relative-value pair ideas within consumer sectors.
insights.quote: they are ten times more likely to do so than their underperforming peers in the same sectors—quietly changing the game while rivals sleep
insights.locator: It’s early in the AI era

insights.claim: A company's AI strategic context is set by two axes: whether AI threatens its business model (disruption) and whether it can serve new AI-driven demand or use AI as a growth accelerator (opportunity), yielding four archetypes.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: Map portfolio holdings onto the 2x2 to separate AI beneficiaries, self-disruptors, pivot candidates, and AI-neutral operators.

insights.claim: Business models built on capability-based advantages such as talent and customer insight are more likely to be disrupted by AI than those with position-based advantages such as brand and resource access.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: Favor moats rooted in brands and scarce physical assets over knowledge/talent moats when underwriting AI disruption risk.
insights.quote: business models that rely on capability-based competitive advantages (for example, talent, customer insight) are more likely to be disrupted by AI than those with position-based advantages (for example, brand, resource access)
insights.locator: The degree of AI disruption risk

insights.claim: Beyond semiconductors, software, and computing hardware, REITs controlling potential data center sites, utilities supplying energy, and telcos providing connectivity benefit from tailwinds of the AI build-out.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: Second-order AI build-out plays include land/REITs, power utilities, and telcos, not just chipmakers.
insights.locator: Semiconductors, software, and computing hardware clearly benefit

insights.claim: Past disruptive technologies show demand shifting in stages: in electrification/mass manufacturing, machine tool makers like Brown & Sharpe benefited first, then mass producers like Ford and Heywood-Wakefield, and finally consumer channels like Sears' catalog.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: Expect AI value capture to rotate over time from infrastructure suppliers toward applications and consumer-facing businesses.
insights.locator: If past disruptive technologies are a guide

insights.claim: Internet-era benefits flowed first to infrastructure (fiber, servers, routers), then e-commerce, and ultimately search, streaming, social networks, and SaaS — implying AI demand will similarly evolve beyond today's build-out into follow-on areas like AI integration services, security, and robotics.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: Position for the next leg of AI demand (integration, security, robotics) as infrastructure spend matures.
insights.quote: over time, it is expected to drive follow-on demand in areas like AI integration services, security, robotics, and more
insights.locator: Similarly, with the advent of the internet

insights.claim: Companies positioned to serve AI build-out demand (construction, data center equipment, semiconductors, energy solutions) should raise growth ambition and ruthlessly prioritize demand pools by size, profitability, and right to win, while hedging to retain attractive non-AI customers.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: Watch whether AI-exposed suppliers are neglecting legacy customers — a concentration risk if AI capex slows.
insights.locator: Positioned to benefit from the AI build-out?

insights.claim: During the dot-com bubble many fiber optic players bet everything on internet demand and, when it burst, found they had lost touch with traditional customers — a warning for AI build-out suppliers today.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: AI infrastructure suppliers with heavy AI revenue concentration carry dot-com-style bust risk; reward those preserving diversified customer bases.
insights.quote: don’t put all your eggs in one basket. During the dot-com era, many fiber optic players did just that
insights.locator: Importantly, don’t put all your eggs

insights.claim: Software firms in CRM, ERP, and similar categories whose knowledge-based advantages are vulnerable to AI must self-disrupt and reimagine offerings as AI-first before AI-first upstarts or rivals do.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: Incumbent enterprise software faces existential AI-native competition; assess each vendor's AI-first transition and its talent, compute, and data plans.
insights.quote: Could an AI-first upstart eat your lunch? Reinvent the core.
insights.locator: Could an AI-first upstart eat your lunch?

insights.claim: Denial is the critical pitfall for disrupted incumbents: Blockbuster had a strong brand and loyal customers but failed to move decisively into online rentals and lost to Netflix, while Walmart methodically built an online business.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: Brand loyalty is not a defense against technology disruption; penalize incumbents slow to reinvent.

insights.claim: Business process outsourcing companies could be disrupted by agentic AI commoditizing their offerings and may need to pivot beyond the core into adjacent value pools using M&A and partnerships.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: BPO is a prime AI-disruption short/watch list; look for credible pivots or M&A as catalysts.
insights.quote: Many business process outsourcing companies, for example, could find themselves disrupted by the rise of agentic AI—and need to chart a new course.
insights.locator: Does AI threaten to erase your advantage?

insights.claim: Fujifilm survived digital photography by redeploying its chemicals and advanced materials expertise into health care, cosmetics, and advanced electronics — the model for pivoting when AI commoditizes a core business.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: When evaluating disrupted firms, focus on which durable capabilities can be redeployed into adjacent markets.
insights.locator: Fujifilm’s response to the rise of digital photography

themes.theme: Step up your game: AI as accelerator

insights.claim: For sectors like consumer staples and durables where AI is neither a market opportunity nor a threat, the winning approach is to use AI function by function to raise innovation hit rates, go-to-market effectiveness, and order-to-delivery speed, prioritized by ROI.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: In AI-neutral sectors, look for firms reinvesting AI-driven gains into advantage rather than superficial adoption.
insights.locator: Does AI pose neither a market opportunity nor a threat?

insights.claim: Domino's won by reorienting its entire go-to-market around digital channels, which now represent more than 85% of its US sales, even though other pizza companies may have launched apps earlier — showing that whole-business reorientation beats 'checking the box' adoption.
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: Judge AI adoption by depth of business-model change, not by first-mover tool launches.
insights.quote: today, mobile and online represent more than 85% of its US sales

insights.claim: BCG argues real AI value comes not from broad deployment for everyday tasks but from reshaping end-to-end workflows and inventing new offerings or business models (the deploy, reshape, invent framework).
insights.speaker: Justin Manly
insights.so_what: Discount companies touting AI tool rollouts; reward evidence of workflow redesign and new AI-enabled revenue lines.
insights.locator: BCG highlights three ways organizations embrace AI
